Debates in Zoological Classification: Although all zoologists use the same system of classifying animals, they do not always agree on how the classification should be done (p. 13).
Backboned Animals in Chordata: All animals with backbones belong to the phylum Chordata (p. 13).

pamphlet_excerpts: Vast Diversity of Animal Life: A million or more different kinds of animals are now alive (p. 13).
Need for Scientific Naming: The scientist needs to have an orderly way to identify animals by name (p. 13).
Grouping by Shared Traits: The system of classification was developed to separate animals by their differences and groups them according to the ways they are alike (p. 13).
Pouched Marsupial Birth Traits: Marsupials, like the kangaroo (right) and the opossum, give birth to young (p. 13).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Group Animals by Shared Traits: The system of classification was developed to separate animals by their differences and groups them according to the ways they are alike (p. 13).
Step 2 - Distinguish Marsupial Birth Patterns: Marsupials, like the kangaroo (right) and the opossum, give birth to young (p. 13).
Step 3 - Observe Pouch and Fur Protection: Young in many species typically are protected by a pouch (marsupium), while others cling to the mother's fur (p. 13).
Step 4 - Trace Nursing Inside the Marsupium: When the young are born, they find their way to the mother'snipples, which may be protected by a marsupium (p. 13).

pamphlet_excerpts: Long-Term Shared Wildlife Trails: Animals may share a single pathway through the woods, across a meadow, or up a hillside, and use that trail for many years (p. 27).
Tracks, Scat, and Hair Clues: Look for evidence of animal tracks, droppings, and hair on any well-used pathway through the brush (p. 27).
Choosing Off-Trail Observation Spots: Find a secluded spot a little bit off the trail to observe the mammals that pass (p. 27).
Keeping Distance From Active Trails: Be careful not to get too close to the trail so as not to spook the animals that use (p. 27).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Select an Off-Trail Vantage Point: Find a secluded spot a little bit off the trail to observe the mammals that pass (p. 27).
Step 2 - Maintain Quiet Distance From Trails: Be careful not to get too close to the trail so as not to spook the animals that use (p. 27).
Step 3 - Inspect Rubbings, Gnawing, and Scratchings: Evidence of mammals also may be found in signs of rubbings, gnawing, and scratching (p. 27).
